Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONDON, England (CNN) -- Protesters draped themselves in the colorful flag of Tibet and shouted slogans at the Chinese embassy in London on Saturday at the start of a demonstration to mark the 50th anniversary since the Tibetan uprising against China. Protesters have gathered in London to mark the 50th anniversary of the Tibet uprising. "Tibetans in Tibet -- we are with you!" they shouted. "China, China, China -- out, out, out!" The small but fervent group marched from the embassy through west London to Trafalgar Square, where they were due to hear a speech by Thomas Shao Jiang, a Chinese dissident who was one of the student organizers of the Tiananmen Square protest in Beijing in 1989. "I think it's important that Tibet is kept in the world's eye," protester Chris Last told CNN amid placards declaring "50 years too long" and "We are Tibetans, not Chinese." While Tibet is technically autonomous from the central Chinese government, its current government is directed from Beijing. The Dalai Lama, traditionally the spiritual and political leader of the Tibetan Buddhists, lives in exile in India. Tuesday marks the 50th anniversary of a failed 1959 uprising against Beijing's rule that sent the Dalai Lama into exile. Protest organizers said the march was meant to draw public attention to what they say is a deepening crisis a year after China cracked down on protests across Tibet. "(British Prime Minister) Gordon Brown and other world leaders must respond urgently and publicly to the Tibet crisis by taking immediate action," said Stephanie Brigden, director of Free Tibet. "They should demand that China calls off its security stranglehold in Tibet as an essential first step towards backing the Dalai Lama's initiative in finding a long-term and negotiated settlement to China's occupation." Tibetan Buddhists say they resent the slow erosion of their culture amid an influx of Han Chinese, the largest ethnic group in China. That resentment spilled over last March, when Buddhist monks initiated peaceful anti-Chinese protests in the regional capital, Lhasa, on the 49th anniversary of the uprising. The protests soon turned violent, with demonstrators burning vehicles and shops. Some protesters advocated independence from China, while others demonstrated against the growing influence of the Han Chinese in the area and other regions of China with ethnic Tibetan populations. The subsequent crackdown left 18 civilians and one police officer dead, according to the Chinese government. Tibet's self-proclaimed government-in-exile put the death toll from the protests at 140. China accuses the Dalai Lama of fomenting the discord in his homeland -- a charge he denies. "The Dalai Lama demanded the establishment of the so-called 'Greater Tibetan area' on a quarter of the Chinese territory, to drive away Chinese army stationed there guarding the Chinese territory, and to drive away Chinese people of other ethnic groups who lived there for generations. Is such a person a religious figure?" Chinese Foreign Minister Yang Jiechi said Saturday. "The conflict between him and us is not religious conflict, human rights conflict, ethnic conflict, nor cultural conflict," Yang said. "The conflict is whether or not to maintain China's unification, and whether or not to permit Tibet to be separated from the Chinese territory." The Dalai Lama has said he does not advocate violence or a separate and independent Tibet. He has said he wants a genuine autonomy that preserves the cultural heritage of the region. "I'm just disgusted with the way the Chinese behave towards the Tibetans. Even if you accept that Tibet has been swallowed up by China, why can't they give to them autonomy, respect their religion, their culture?" protester Bob Hunt said Saturday. "These are peaceable people, one of the most peaceable people in the world." Protester Shobha Trivedi said she hoped the protest march would make people more aware of the situation inside Tibet. "I feel as a human being, what (the) Chinese are doing for 50 years, nobody's bothering with it," she said. "And it's a real shame on everyone."

**LONDON, England (CNN) —** Protesters draped themselves in the colorful Tibetan flag and chanted slogans outside the Chinese Embassy in London on Saturday at the start of a demonstration marking the 50th anniversary of the Tibetan uprising against China.

“Tibetans in Tibet — we are with you!” they shouted. “China, China, China — out, out, out!”

The small but fervent group marched from the embassy through west London to Trafalgar Square, where demonstrators were scheduled to hear a speech by Thomas Shao Jiang, a Chinese dissident who was among the student organizers of the 1989 Tiananmen Square protest in Beijing.

“I think it’s important that Tibet is kept in the world’s eye,” protester Chris Last told CNN, surrounded by placards declaring “50 years too long” and “We are Tibetans, not Chinese.”

Although Tibet is technically autonomous from China’s central government, its current government is directed from Beijing. The Dalai Lama, traditionally the spiritual and political leader of Tibetan Buddhists, lives in exile in India.

Tuesday marks the 50th anniversary of the failed 1959 uprising against Beijing’s rule, which forced the Dalai Lama into exile.

Organizers said the march was intended to draw public attention to what they described as a deepening crisis, one year after China cracked down on protests across Tibet.

“[British Prime Minister] Gordon Brown and other world leaders must respond urgently and publicly to the Tibet crisis by taking immediate action,” said Stephanie Brigden, director of Free Tibet.

“They should demand that China calls off its security stranglehold in Tibet as an essential first step towards backing the Dalai Lama’s initiative in finding a long-term and negotiated settlement to China’s occupation.”

Tibetan Buddhists say they resent the gradual erosion of their culture amid an influx of Han Chinese, China’s largest ethnic group.

That resentment spilled over in March of last year, when Buddhist monks initiated peaceful anti-Chinese protests in the regional capital, Lhasa, on the 49th anniversary of the uprising. The protests soon turned violent, with demonstrators setting fire to vehicles and shops.

Some protesters advocated independence from China, while others demonstrated against the growing influence of Han Chinese in Tibet and in other regions of China with ethnic Tibetan populations.

According to the Chinese government, the subsequent crackdown left 18 civilians and one police officer dead. Tibet’s self-proclaimed government-in-exile put the protest death toll at 140.

China accuses the Dalai Lama of fomenting unrest in his homeland, a charge he denies.

“The Dalai Lama demanded the establishment of the so-called ‘Greater Tibetan area’ on a quarter of the Chinese territory, to drive away Chinese army stationed there guarding the Chinese territory, and to drive away Chinese people of other ethnic groups who lived there for generations. Is such a person a religious figure?” Chinese Foreign Minister Yang Jiechi said Saturday.

“The conflict between him and us is not religious conflict, human rights conflict, ethnic conflict, nor cultural conflict,” Yang said. “The conflict is whether or not to maintain China’s unification, and whether or not to permit Tibet to be separated from the Chinese territory.”

The Dalai Lama has said he does not advocate violence or a separate, independent Tibet. He has said he seeks genuine autonomy that would preserve the region’s cultural heritage.

“I’m just disgusted with the way the Chinese behave towards the Tibetans. Even if you accept that Tibet has been swallowed up by China, why can’t they give to them autonomy, respect their religion, their culture?” protester Bob Hunt said Saturday. “These are peaceable people, one of the most peaceable people in the world.”

Protester Shobha Trivedi said she hoped the march would raise awareness of the situation inside Tibet.

“I feel as a human being, what [the] Chinese are doing for 50 years, nobody’s bothering with it,” she said. “And it’s a real shame on everyone.”
outputs.L2:
LONDON, England (CNN) — Wearing bright Tibetan flags and chanting outside China’s embassy in London, demonstrators began a Saturday march commemorating 50 years since the Tibetan revolt against Chinese rule.

“Tibetans in Tibet — we are with you!” the protesters called out, followed by chants demanding that China leave Tibet.

Though relatively few in number, the passionate participants walked from the embassy across west London toward Trafalgar Square. There, Thomas Shao Jiang—a Chinese dissident who helped organize the 1989 Tiananmen Square student demonstrations in Beijing—was scheduled to address them.

Participant Chris Last told CNN that keeping international attention focused on Tibet was essential. Around him, signs carried messages including “50 years too long” and “We are Tibetans, not Chinese.”

Tibet officially has autonomous status, but its administration is controlled by the central government in Beijing. The Dalai Lama, regarded traditionally as Tibetan Buddhism’s spiritual and political leader, remains exiled in India.

Tuesday will be the 50th anniversary of the unsuccessful 1959 rebellion against Beijing’s authority, after which the Dalai Lama fled into exile.

Those organizing the London event said its purpose was to raise awareness of what they described as an increasingly serious crisis, one year after Chinese authorities suppressed demonstrations throughout Tibet.

Stephanie Brigden, director of Free Tibet, urged British Prime Minister Gordon Brown and other international leaders to take immediate, visible action. She said they should first press Beijing to end its tight security measures in Tibet and then support the Dalai Lama’s effort to reach a lasting settlement through negotiation over what she called China’s occupation.

Tibetan Buddhists say the arrival of growing numbers of Han Chinese—China’s largest ethnic population—is gradually weakening their culture and has created deep resentment.

Those tensions erupted in March of the previous year. On the uprising’s 49th anniversary, Buddhist monks launched peaceful protests against Chinese rule in Lhasa, the regional capital. Violence later broke out, and demonstrators set fire to stores and vehicles.

Some participants called for Tibet to become independent, while others objected to the increasing Han Chinese presence both in Tibet and in other Chinese regions inhabited by ethnic Tibetans.

According to China’s government, the crackdown that followed resulted in the deaths of 18 civilians and one police officer. Tibet’s declared government-in-exile, however, said 140 people died during the unrest.

Beijing alleges that the Dalai Lama instigated instability in Tibet, an accusation he rejects.

Chinese Foreign Minister Yang Jiechi said Saturday that the Dalai Lama had sought the creation of a so-called “Greater Tibetan area” covering one-quarter of China. Yang also accused him of wanting Chinese troops removed from that territory and people belonging to other ethnic communities—many of whom had lived there for generations—expelled. He questioned whether someone making such demands could be considered a religious leader.

Yang argued that the disagreement was not about religion, human rights, ethnicity or culture. Instead, he characterized it as a dispute over preserving China’s unity and preventing Tibet from being detached from Chinese territory.

The Dalai Lama has stated that he opposes violence and is not seeking an independent, separate Tibet. Rather, he says his goal is meaningful autonomy that would safeguard the region’s cultural traditions.

At Saturday’s demonstration, Bob Hunt said he was appalled by China’s treatment of Tibetans. Even if Tibet’s incorporation into China were accepted, he argued, Beijing should still allow Tibetans autonomy and show respect for their religion and culture. He described Tibetans as peaceful people—among the most peaceful in the world.

Another demonstrator, Shobha Trivedi, said she hoped the march would increase public understanding of conditions within Tibet. Speaking from a humanitarian perspective, she said China’s actions over the previous five decades had largely been ignored and called that neglect shameful for everyone.

counterfactuals.output:
# “Free Tibet”: London Protest Marks 50 Years Since the Tibetan Uprising

In March 2009, several hundred Tibetan exiles and their supporters gathered outside the Chinese Embassy in London to commemorate the 50th anniversary of the 1959 Tibetan uprising. The demonstration, held in the days surrounding the March 10 anniversary, was part remembrance ceremony and part political protest, drawing attention to continuing restrictions in Tibet and to the security crackdown that had followed unrest across Tibetan regions a year earlier.

The embassy on Portland Place became the focal point for a crowd carrying Tibetan flags, photographs of the Dalai Lama and placards demanding political and religious freedom. Demonstrators repeatedly chanted **“Free Tibet,” “China out of Tibet,”** and **“Long live the Dalai Lama.”** Other slogans called for an end to repression and urged Beijing to enter meaningful negotiations with Tibetan representatives.

Police maintained barriers around the diplomatic compound and monitored the gathering. The event was largely peaceful, though the atmosphere outside the embassy was impassioned, reflecting anger over reports that Tibetan areas had been placed under especially tight controls before the anniversary.

## From the Chinese Embassy to Trafalgar Square

After demonstrating outside the embassy, protesters formed a procession through central London and marched toward Trafalgar Square. Tibetan flags and banners made the march highly visible, while chants continued along the route. Participants included members of Britain’s Tibetan community, Buddhist supporters, human-rights campaigners and activists from groups such as Free Tibet and the Tibet Society.

At Trafalgar Square, speakers recalled the events of March 1959, when an uprising against Chinese rule erupted in Lhasa. Chinese forces suppressed the revolt, and the Dalai Lama fled across the Himalayas into India, where the Tibetan government-in-exile was later established.

The London rally also focused heavily on more recent events. In March 2008, protests had begun in Lhasa and spread to other Tibetan-populated areas of China. Beijing said rioting had killed civilians and damaged shops and public property. Tibetan groups maintained that the subsequent security campaign involved mass arrests, disappearances, harsh prison sentences and severe restrictions on monasteries, communications and travel.

Campaigners in London argued that the anniversary could not be treated only as a historical commemoration. They described it as evidence of an unresolved political conflict and appealed to the British government and other Western governments to press China over human rights.

## Tibetan Activists’ Response

Tibetan activists said the demonstration was intended to show that the Tibetan question had not disappeared despite China’s efforts to prevent protests inside Tibet. For many participants, the freedom to march in London contrasted sharply with conditions in Tibetan regions, where public displays of the Tibetan flag or support for the Dalai Lama could lead to detention.

Activists accused the Chinese authorities of suppressing Tibetan religion, language and national identity. They also criticized the system of political education in monasteries, restrictions on images of the Dalai Lama and Beijing’s influence over the recognition of senior Buddhist figures.

Some demonstrators called openly for Tibetan independence, as reflected in the slogan “China out of Tibet.” Others supported the Dalai Lama’s stated “Middle Way” policy, which sought genuine autonomy rather than separation from China. Under that proposal, Tibet would remain within the People’s Republic of China but would receive greater control over culture, education, religion and environmental policy.

Speakers urged Beijing to resume substantive talks with the Dalai Lama’s envoys. They argued that previous rounds of contact had produced little progress because Chinese officials refused to consider meaningful self-government.

## Beijing’s Position

Chinese officials rejected the protesters’ account of Tibet’s modern history. Beijing maintained that Tibet was an inseparable part of China and described the 1959 events not as a national uprising but as a rebellion led by members of the old Tibetan ruling class.

According to the Chinese government, its actions in 1959 ended a system of “feudal serfdom” dominated by aristocrats and monasteries. Officials pointed to economic development, improved infrastructure, longer life expectancy and increased access to education and health care as evidence that Chinese rule had benefited Tibetans.

Chinese representatives also rejected claims that Beijing was attempting to destroy Tibetan culture or Buddhism. They said religious practice was protected by law but had to take place within the Chinese legal and political system.

On the unrest of 2008, Chinese officials emphasized attacks on civilians, businesses and public buildings, accusing supporters of the Dalai Lama of encouraging separatism and violence. Beijing routinely referred to overseas campaign groups as part of a foreign-backed attempt to split China and warned other governments not to interfere in what it regarded as an internal matter.

The Chinese government disputed the Dalai Lama’s claim that he sought only autonomy, arguing that his proposals amounted to independence in all but name. Officials said talks could proceed only if he clearly abandoned separatism and accepted Chinese sovereignty over Tibet and other Tibetan-populated areas.

## Competing Narratives

The London demonstration highlighted two sharply opposed interpretations of Tibet.

For the protesters, March 1959 represented a popular revolt against occupation, followed by decades of political control, cultural pressure and religious repression. The march to Trafalgar Square was therefore both a memorial to those killed or forced into exile and a demand for international action.

For Beijing, the anniversary marked the defeat of an attempt to preserve an oppressive social order. Chinese officials presented the changes introduced after 1959 as democratic reform and liberation, later establishing March 28 as “Serfs’ Emancipation Day.”

Those competing narratives shaped reactions to the London protest. Tibetan activists treated its visibility as especially important at a time when demonstrations inside Tibet were difficult and dangerous. Chinese officials, by contrast, viewed overseas rallies and pro-independence slogans as confirmation that foreign campaigners were supporting separatism.

The procession from the Chinese Embassy to Trafalgar Square did not alter either side’s position. It did, however, place the dispute before the British public at a symbolically significant moment—50 years after the Lhasa uprising and one year after Tibet had again become the focus of international protest and diplomatic controversy.

counterfactuals.output:
### London rally highlights Tibet’s disputed history

Pro-Tibet demonstrators gathered in London, calling for greater religious and political freedoms in Tibet and drawing attention to the anniversaries of the 1959 uprising and the unrest that swept Tibetan areas in 2008.

The rally commemorated 10 March 1959, when thousands of Tibetans surrounded the Dalai Lama’s residence in Lhasa amid fears that Chinese authorities planned to detain him. The protests developed into an uprising against Chinese rule, which had expanded after People’s Liberation Army troops entered Tibet in 1950. Chinese forces suppressed the revolt, although accounts of the fighting and the number killed remain sharply contested.

The Dalai Lama, then 23, escaped Lhasa on 17 March 1959 and crossed into India, where he was granted asylum. He later established a government-in-exile in Dharamsala. Beijing regards him as a separatist, while he says he seeks meaningful autonomy rather than independence. He transferred his formal political authority to an elected exile leadership in 2011 but remains Tibetan Buddhism’s most prominent figure.

Speakers also recalled the unrest that began in Lhasa in March 2008 and spread to other Tibetan-populated regions. The casualty figures remain disputed because access for independent observers was restricted. Chinese authorities said rioters killed 18 civilians and one police officer in Lhasa, emphasizing attacks on Han Chinese and Hui Muslim residents and businesses. Tibetan exile groups said the security crackdown across Tibet and neighboring provinces killed more than 200 Tibetans; some early estimates were lower, at about 140. Beijing rejected those claims and said its forces exercised restraint.

The competing totals refer to different victims, geographic areas and periods, and none has been independently verified in full. That disagreement remains central to the wider dispute: China says Tibet has benefited from development and stability, while Tibetan campaigners allege political repression, restrictions on religion and erosion of language and culture.

counterfactuals.output:
**World leaders urged to act over China’s Tibet crackdown**

**LONDON, March 2008** — Demonstrators and Tibetan campaigners have called on British Prime Minister Gordon Brown and other world leaders to condemn China’s crackdown in Tibet, as protests surrounding the Beijing Olympics intensify international scrutiny of the Chinese government.

Protesters gathered outside the Chinese Embassy in London, chanting “Free Tibet” and “China out of Tibet,” while demanding an end to the use of force against Tibetans. Similar demonstrations took place in cities around the world following unrest in Lhasa and reports that Chinese security forces had moved to suppress protests across Tibetan areas.

Stephanie Brigden, director of the Free Tibet Campaign, urged Brown and other leaders to exert immediate diplomatic pressure on Beijing.

“We are calling on Gordon Brown to make a public statement condemning the Chinese government’s actions,” Brigden said. “The international community must act now and put pressure on China to end the crackdown.”

China has blamed supporters of the Dalai Lama for orchestrating the violence and says its security forces are acting to restore order. Chinese Foreign Minister Yang Jiechi rejected accusations that Beijing was trying to eradicate Tibetan identity.

“The so-called cultural genocide in Tibet is nothing but a lie,” Yang said, accusing the “Dalai clique” of seeking to politicize the Beijing Olympic Games.

Chinese authorities said rioters in Lhasa attacked civilians and burned shops and buildings. Tibetan groups, however, said security forces had used lethal force and that the number of deaths was considerably higher than Beijing acknowledged. Independent verification remained difficult because of restrictions on journalists and access to Tibetan regions.

Campaigners called for China to allow foreign media and independent observers into Tibet, release detained protesters and begin substantive talks with the Dalai Lama’s representatives. They also urged leaders attending Olympic events in Beijing to use their presence as leverage.

Brown faced growing pressure to raise Tibet directly with Chinese leaders and to reconsider his participation in the Olympic ceremonies. Other governments expressed concern but stopped short of supporting a full boycott, arguing that continued engagement offered the best prospect of influencing Beijing.

The dispute placed Tibet at the centre of debate over whether China’s hosting of the Olympics should be separated from its human-rights record. For demonstrators in London, the answer was clear: “No justice, no peace,” they chanted. “Free Tibet.”

## Tibet Uprising Anniversary Highlights Competing Claims Over Autonomy and Unity

**DHARAMSALA, India — March 10, 2009** — Tibetans and their supporters marked the 50th anniversary of the 1959 uprising against Chinese rule on Tuesday, drawing renewed attention to disputes over political autonomy, religious freedom and cultural preservation.

Commemorations were held in Dharamsala, the Indian headquarters of Tibet’s government-in-exile, and in cities around the world. Participants carried Tibetan flags and portraits of the Dalai Lama, who fled Tibet after Chinese forces suppressed the uprising in Lhasa.

Many protesters said Chinese policies have weakened Tibetan language, religious institutions and traditional ways of life. They also expressed concern that economic development and migration into Tibetan areas have left Tibetans with limited influence over local government, education and employment.

The Dalai Lama has said he is seeking “meaningful autonomy” within China rather than independence. His representatives have called for greater Tibetan control over cultural, educational and religious affairs, while leaving foreign policy and defense to Beijing.

China rejects accusations that it is destroying Tibetan culture. The government says its rule ended a feudal system, expanded education and health care, improved transportation and raised living standards. It maintains that Tibet has autonomy under Chinese law and that investment has brought substantial economic gains.

Beijing describes the Dalai Lama as a separatist whose activities threaten China’s sovereignty and national unity. Chinese officials say his autonomy proposals would amount to disguised independence and could separate a large portion of Chinese territory from central authority. The Dalai Lama disputes that characterization and says he supports a negotiated settlement within the People’s Republic of China.

The anniversary came one year after protests spread across Tibetan regions in March 2008. Some demonstrations turned violent, particularly in Lhasa, where rioters attacked civilians and businesses. Chinese security forces conducted a broad crackdown, and rights organizations reported arrests, deaths and restrictions on access. Beijing said it acted to restore order and accused forces associated with the Dalai Lama of organizing the unrest, an allegation he denied.

Security was tightened across Tibet and neighboring Tibetan-populated areas ahead of Tuesday’s anniversary, while access for foreign journalists and visitors was restricted.

The events commemorated began on March 10, 1959, when thousands gathered in Lhasa amid fears that Chinese authorities planned to detain the Dalai Lama. The confrontation developed into an uprising that was crushed by Chinese forces. The Dalai Lama subsequently crossed into India, where he established a government-in-exile.

Fifty years later, the anniversary underscored the continuing divide between Tibetans seeking stronger safeguards for their identity and Beijing’s insistence that territorial integrity and political stability cannot be compromised. Several rounds of talks between Chinese officials and the Dalai Lama’s representatives have failed to produce an agreement, leaving the central questions of autonomy, culture and political authority unresolved.
